title: Four Parenting Tips Schools Can Promote
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. synthesizes four evidence-informed recommendations from Jonathan Haidt, Will Johnson, and Zach Rausch arguing that a majority of parents already want to curb children's smartphone and social media use, and that collective action is what makes individual family efforts possible. The four norms are: delay smartphones until high school, delay social media until age 16, ban phones bell-to-bell including lunch and recess, and redirect after-school time toward real-world independent activity. Stuart frames these not as personal parenting advice but as school-communicable norms that educators can share in newsletters and parent nights, reinforcing the point that school-family partnerships face far less friction than individual families acting alone.
points: The article's foundational argument is collective efficacy: social norms require critical mass, and polling data shows large majorities of parents already share these goals, reducing the political difficulty of adoption.

Delaying smartphones until high school (favored by two-thirds of polled parents) and social media until 16 (73 percent support) are presented not as radical proposals but as already-majority positions.

Bell-to-bell phone bans including lunch and recess, supported by 63 percent of parents, go further than most current school policies — Stuart notes his own school's classroom phone garages fall short.
Schools serve as natural coordination points for establishing parenting norms that individual families cannot sustain alone, an argument Stuart extends to legislative action as a complementary tool.
The researchers' framing of the ultimate goal as 'restoring childhood' repositions phone restriction as an affirmative vision rather than merely a prohibition.
quotes: I came across four parent recommendations the other day from researchers Jonathan Haidt, Will Johnson, and Zach Rausch that I thought were worth sharing in case your role intersects with helping parents in our technological times. In their article for The New York Times, the trio explains that a majority of parents think their children's childhood would be better without a lot of the internet things us teachers see affecting student engagement.

It's hard for any one parent or school to act alone, but when families and schools act together, change becomes possible. These norms are meant to reinforce one another, and when combined, they offer a road map for reclaiming a healthier and more joyful childhood.

As a parent of two teenagers myself, the authors are right: aiming at these goals as individual families is much more labor-intensive than doing so with a pod of parents. Social norms are powerful. This is why clear, consistent, and admin-led cell phone policies are critical in schools.

So, these may be worth sharing in your next parent newsletter or school/parent night. As you do so, be mindful that parenting is hard and that the polling data indicates these ideas are quite popular. Difficult, but popular.
The goal, the authors conclude, isn't just to limit screens. It's much bigger than that. The goal is to restore childhood.
